source.title: The Expert Strikes Back: Interpreting Mixture-of-Experts Language Models at Expert Level
source.authors: Jeremy Herbst; Jae Hee Lee; Stefan Wermter

record.tranche_reason: The study uses k-sparse probing rather than a pole-by-pole job audit. Its held-out probe results directly address neuron-level polysemanticity across dense and MoE models, but do not estimate the claim’s percentages.
record.gate_note: The study probes concepts using held-out data and reports best-layer F1 results across models and k values. The rows below retain the k=1 figure results for each model, the setting most relevant to single-neuron interpretability. Automatic expert-label scores and expert-level causal-attribution results are recorded separately as findings that fit no listed version; they do not test the claimed neuron-pole shares. Literature results cited by the paper are not included.
record.test_reason: The study uses k-sparse probing (k=1 best-layer F1) to compare single-neuron concept concentration in 6 dense and 6 MoE language models. It concludes that dense FFN neurons are more polysemantic than MoE expert neurons, that the gap grows with routing sparsity, and that architecture rather than parameter count drives it (OLMo family). This bears on V2 (whether similar cleanliness holds across dense and MoE models) and on the architecture-not-capacity part of V4. It is only a proxy: it asks whether some neuron captures each of 58 concepts, not what share of neurons have one job.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that MoE expert neurons are less polysemantic than dense FFN neurons, more so with sparser routing and not explained by parameter count. They regard dense neurons as largely uninterpretable and argue that whole experts are interpretable 'fine-grained task experts', validated by automatic labels and DLA attribution. They state experts are not entirely monosemantic.
record.recipe_differences: Uses k-sparse linear probes to compare concept concentration in neurons, then automatically labels and scores whole experts and evaluates expert-level attribution. It does not reproduce the cited neuron-pole audit or its job-counting procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The results vary with routing sparsity; the paper reports cleaner representations for sparser MoEs and lower scores for denser MoEs. Probe performance is shown across k values, with the largest MoE–dense gap at k=1.

fits_no_version.finding: LLM-generated labels for whole MoE experts mostly score F1>0.8 on held-out detection, highest for the sparsest model. Five selected failures score 0.18–0.46.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Whole MoE experts can be described by short natural-language labels that a scorer LLM can apply to held-out examples, with reliability rising with routing sparsity.

fits_no_version.finding: On label-derived synthetic prompts, the matched OLMoE expert usually ranks Top-1 to Top-8 in DLA for the target word. In 80% of control prompts it is not routed at all.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Expert-level labels in OLMoE predict expert routing and direct logit contribution on new prompts.

record.problems: The study does not measure the claimed pole-level job shares. Best-layer selection is an upper-bound strategy, and MoE probes are evaluated on tokens already routed to the target expert. Expert-label scores are produced by an LLM scorer; the paper documents several failure cases and analyzes only selected layers for the expert-level study. The largest current MoE models, including DeepSeek-V3, were not included. Many plotted probe results have no exact values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: The per-model k-sparse curves at k=2, 4, 8, 16, 32, and 64 are figure-only and were not extracted; the retained probe rows cover k=1 for each model. These omitted curve points appear in Figures 1, 3, and 8. Specialization-score tables and further expert case studies concern expert-level routing/output distributions rather than neuron-pole shares.

untested.parts: There is no pole-by-pole job audit and no Qwen3-32B. There are no 90%/7%/2–4% shares.
There are no estimates of per-neuron job shares. No model approaches trillions of parameters (DeepSeek-V3 was excluded).
There is no InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron, pose analysis or recursive-generalization account.
There are no vision models and no 5%→99% estimates. The roles of regularization and tool quality are not isolated.
There are no neuron-based attribution graphs and no comparison with replacement-model reconstruction error. The attribution is at expert level.
No neuron explanation is tested against where the neuron fires. Label failure cases concern whole experts.
There is no simulation-based scoring of neuron explanations. Detection scoring is applied to expert labels only.

missing.what: Routing-sparsity comparison of best-layer F1 across NA/N groups (0.06, 0.08, 0.12, 0.25), the main evidence that cleanliness scales with architecture
Per-concept-category MoE vs dense scatter; text says nearly every point lies above the equality line
Statement that dense-model variance across concepts is larger and some concepts are poorly represented in dense models

record.verdict_notes: The study's framing contradicts the essay's premise for dense models: the authors call dense neurons uninterpretable and superposed. Its evidence, however, is a k=1 best-neuron probe over 58 regex/POS concepts with best-layer and best-expert selection, which cannot yield a share of clean neurons. Hence limits_scope rather than challenges for V2. All probe values are figure-only, so the states are set from the text's qualitative statements. Expert-level scoring resembles V7's method but applies to experts, so it is kept out of V7. The Qwen model is 30B-A3B, not V1's 32B dense model.

versions.untested_parts: The paper studies Qwen3-30B-A3B, not Qwen3-32B, and does not count neuron poles assigned one job, two related jobs, or not-yet-understood jobs.
It probes 12 models, but does not estimate the claimed shares of poles, test models up to trillions of parameters, or establish that the numerical shares are similar across models.
No InceptionV1 cat-and-car example, pose interpretation, or recursive-generalization account is tested.
The study does not test InceptionV1-sized vision models, compare the essay’s estimates, or isolate architecture, regularization, and tool quality as causes of interpretability.
It tests expert-level descriptions and attribution, not neuron-based attribution graphs or reconstruction error from a trained replacement model.
It does not test neuron explanations against where individual neurons fire; its explanation scoring is at the MoE expert level.
It does not score neuron explanations by simulating neuron activations on new text; its automated scores concern expert-level labels.

relationships.condition: Dense FFN models and the densest MoE (Mixtral)

relationships.display_finding: Dense models struggled at k=1, MoE models beat dense ones in every category, and Mixtral scored below sparser MoEs. Single-unit cleanliness therefore depends on routing sparsity, though the paper gives only the direction, not numbers.

relation.reason: Its own results bear on V2 and V4.

tranche.reason: k-sparse probes on dense vs MoE neurons are a different method on the same polysemanticity question.

source_check.notes: Probe values are figure-only. MoE probes use only tokens routed to the target expert, and best-layer/best-expert selection is an upper bound. The text states no k for the category comparison (Fig 2) or the OLMo-family comparison (Fig 3). Tying them to k=1 is the record's framing, which fits Sec 4.2's statement that the gap is largest at k=1. Rows r13-r22 link to no version, so their states are not version-checked.

statements.correction: Sec 4.1: MoE probe data are filtered to tokens routed to the target expert (router acts as a coarse filter); dense probes have no such filter. Sec 4.2: best-layer (best-expert) selection is an upper bound.
statements.problem: Mentions a caveat about which tokens MoE probes use without saying what it is, and shows the pipeline note '(truncated in pack)' to readers.
Minor: the study's dense comparators also include OLMo-1B/7B (SwiGLU) and pythia-12b (GELU, Table 2). It reports no GELU vs SwiGLU dense comparison, so the untested line stands.
Minor: the probed units are the experts' hidden intermediate neurons h (Eq. 1). The mismatch for this study is the concept-probe measure with best-layer/expert selection, not the unit.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: The authors report that MoE experts often achieve near-optimal F1 at k=1 and that MoE models outperform dense counterparts; this supports the broader monosemanticity direction, but not the claimed numerical shares (r7-r12).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Dense-versus-MoE comparisons in the tested models
reader_labels.reason: The authors explicitly report a performance gap between MoE and dense probes, including that dense models struggle at k=1 and that OLMoE-1B-7B outperforms OLMo-7B despite the dense model having 7× more active parameters per token. These proxy results do not show similar interpretability across dense and MoE models (r1-r8).
